verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.13.38 (BORI critical edition, Aranyaka Parva); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XII. Our id 3.12.46 follows a vulgate-style count: chapter agrees with Ganguli, verse number does not match BORI.
attribution_note: Krishna to Arjuna is correct. The setting can be sharpened: Krishna had just flared up in anger at the Kauravas, and Arjuna's long praise of his deeds was meant to calm him; this verse is Krishna's reply.
translation_note: Accurate. The very next verse (BORI 3.13.39) continues: 'you are Nara, I am Narayana', which is the ground of the bond.
context: Soon after the dice game, Krishna and allied kings visit the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest. Krishna erupts in anger and promises the deaths of Duryodhana, Karna and Shakuni; Arjuna soothes him by reciting Krishna's divine deeds. Krishna answers with this declaration of mutual belonging and adds that the two of them are the ancient sages Nara and Narayana. Draupadi then comes forward and pours out her grief to him.

key_terms.sense: you are mine alone, I am yours alone
those who belong to me, my people
the paired sages; Arjuna and Krishna as one being in two forms

core_teaching: Krishna declares a complete, two-way bond with Arjuna: whatever belongs to one belongs to the other, and their friends and enemies are shared. The epic grounds this in their identity as Nara and Narayana rather than in mere friendship.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as a pledge of mutual possession and shared friends and foes, then moves straight into the Nara-Narayana identity, so the bond reads as metaphysical kinship, not only affection.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: The verse stands unchanged in the constituted text at 3.13.38, followed by the Nara-Narayana verse. A near-identical line recurs in Udyoga 5.89.28, where Krishna says whoever hates the Pandavas hates him.

practical_reading: Read devotionally, it says the one who turns to God is held as God's own, not as a stranger. In a human key it describes the kind of friendship where your people become my people.
misreadings: Not a license to treat one's personal opponents as God's enemies; it was spoken while Krishna's anger at the Kauravas was being calmed.
Not a general promise about any human friendship; it rests on the special Nara-Narayana identity.
cautions: 'Whoever hates you hates me' can feed us-versus-them thinking for a reader in an active conflict.
speaks_to: a deep friendship or partnership that feels like kinship
not_for: someone in a feud seeking divine endorsement against another person

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.13.117 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XII. Our verse number 134 is a vulgate-style count.
attribution_note: Krishna to Draupadi in the Kamyaka forest: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. In context the 'word' is a specific promise: the wives of her tormentors will weep over husbands killed by Arjuna's arrows, and she will again be a queen.
context: Draupadi has just recounted the dice hall, being dragged by the hair while menstruating, and every earlier plot against the Pandavas, and has wept that she has no husbands, sons, kin, or even Krishna. Krishna replies that the wives of those she is angry with will weep as she does, that he will do all he can for the Pandavas, and that she will be queen again; this cosmic oath seals it. Arjuna confirms it, and Dhrishtadyumna names who will kill whom.

key_terms.sense: my word will not prove empty

core_teaching: Krishna gives his unbreakable word that the wrong done to Draupadi will be answered. The impossibilities listed stress that the cosmos would break before his promise does.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XII
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli the oath directly follows the promise that her tormentors' wives will weep over their slain husbands and that she will be a queen again, so the vow is about justice through war.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.13.117 matches our Sanskrit. The same second line reappears in a starred passage of Udyoga 5.80, where Krishna renews his word to Draupadi before his peace mission.

practical_reading: Teachers often take it as an image of a promise that holds when everything else gives way; for a reader it can say that someone sees the wrong done to them and will not forget it.
misreadings: Not a call to personal revenge.
Not a promise that a particular outcome will arrive on our timetable.
cautions: In the text the vow foretells killing; keep a reading on 'being seen and stood by', as our misuse note says.
Context includes sexual humiliation and assault on Draupadi; avoid graphic retelling for a distressed reader.
speaks_to: feeling abandoned after being publicly wronged
needing to hear that a promise to you will be kept
not_for: someone nursing a wish for vengeance
a reader who wants a guarantee of a specific result

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.29.25 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXVIII. Our id 3.28.27 follows the vulgate chapter count (one chapter behind BORI here).
attribution_note: Correct nesting: Draupadi quotes Prahlada's reply to his grandson Bali (Vairochani), within Vaishampayana's narration.
translation_note: Our translation ('even badly') follows the vulgate reading aparādhe garīyasi, which Ganguli also renders as a grave wrong. The BORI critical text reads aparādhe 'garīyasi, i.e. 'when the offence is NOT grave'. Debroy's critical-edition rendering (as quoted in Swarajya) likewise limits it to crimes 'not too great'. Suggest: 'If someone who once helped you wrongs you, and the wrong is not too grave, forgive it in light of that help.'
context: In the forest Draupadi presses Yudhishthira to answer the Kauravas with force. She cites Prahlada: neither constant forgiveness nor constant force is right; the always-forgiving are trampled and the never-forgiving are feared like a snake in the house. He then lists the occasions for forgiveness, beginning with this one, and says force belongs to all others. Draupadi concludes that the Kauravas, who wrong them continually, are not a case for forgiveness.

key_terms.sense: one who did you good earlier
in an offence that is grave / (critical text) not grave

core_teaching: Forgiveness has proper occasions; a past benefactor's earlier kindness should weigh in his favour when he offends. In the critical text this applies to offences that are not grave.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli follows the vulgate: a former benefactor is to be forgiven even a serious wrong, out of remembrance of his service. He frames the list as Prahlada's answer that might and forgiveness each have their time.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text has 'garīyasi, 'not too grave', so the critical edition restricts this forgiveness to lesser offences. The next verses: deliberate offenders who plead ignorance are punished even for small faults; a first offence is forgiven, a second is not.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Summarises Prahlada's middle path: forgive a former benefactor if the crime is not too great, forgive stupidity and first offences, examine unintended ones, punish knowing offences; Draupadi says now is not the time for forgiveness.

practical_reading: When someone with a long record of kindness hurts you, their history can rightly count toward giving them another chance, as long as the hurt is not grave or repeated.
misreadings: Not a rule that benefactors, parents or mentors may do anything and must be forgiven.
Draupadi cites it to show forgiveness's limits, not to urge more forgiveness.
cautions: A reader hurt by a parent, partner or patron 'who did so much for you' may hear pressure to excuse serious harm; use the critical reading and the misuse note.
speaks_to: a falling-out with an old friend, mentor or relative after a hurtful act
deciding whether to give a second chance
not_for: abuse or repeated serious harm by a caregiver or benefactor
coercive relationships where past help is used as leverage

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.29.26 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXVIII.
attribution_note: Correct nesting: Prahlada to Bali, quoted by Draupadi to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate. Minor reading differences only (BORI: abuddhim āśritānāṃ ca ... pāṇḍityaṃ).
context: Second item in Prahlada's list of times for forgiveness, quoted by Draupadi. Immediately after it he says that those who offend knowingly and then claim it was unintended should be punished even for a small offence; a first offence is forgiven, a second punished. Draupadi uses the list to argue that the Kauravas fall outside it.

key_terms.sense: those who acted out of lack of understanding

core_teaching: Wrongs born of ignorance or poor judgement deserve forgiveness, because good sense is not easy for anyone to have at all times. Deliberate wrongs dressed up as mistakes do not qualify.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as forgiving offenders who acted from ignorance and folly, since wisdom is hard to come by, and immediately contrasts those who offend knowingly and then plead ignorance, who are not to be pardoned.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Same sense in the constituted text 3.29.26; the following verses 27-29 set the limit (knowing offenders punished, a second offence punished, unintended acts forgiven only after careful inquiry).

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Notes Prahlada's reason: learning is not easily available to people, so offences from stupidity are forgiven, while offences done with full knowledge are punished as crookedness.

practical_reading: Before judging a hurt, ask whether it came from carelessness or ignorance; such mistakes can be met with patience, especially from the young or inexperienced.
misreadings: Not a reason to excuse someone who keeps 'not knowing' after being told.
cautions: Pair with the misuse note: one mistake is different from a pattern of harm.
speaks_to: irritation at someone's clumsy or thoughtless hurt
parents, teachers or managers dealing with others' mistakes
not_for: repeated, knowing harm presented as 'I didn't mean it'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.30.5 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXIX.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Draupadi: correct.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira's reply to Draupadi's call for force. He opens by saying anger is both what destroys people and, when mastered, what makes them prosper; then he lists what the angry do: they sin, kill even their teachers, insult their elders, and cannot tell what should be said. He concludes that one like him cannot indulge such a force.

key_terms.sense: what should and should not be said
angered, in the grip of anger

core_teaching: Anger blinds judgement: under its grip a person loses the sense of limits in speech and action.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli the line sits in a list of anger's effects: the angry man may kill the innocent, honour the guilty, insult superiors, even destroy himself. Yudhishthira uses it to explain why he keeps his own anger down.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.5 is the same. The chapter opens (3.30.1) with the claim that anger is both man's slayer and, if mastered, his prosperer.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Summarises Yudhishthira's counsel: an angry person cannot see the right course or his own limits; the author adds that this forbearance looks like calculation, and that Draupadi and Bhima reject it.

practical_reading: When anger rises, delay speaking and acting; words said in that state are the ones most often regretted.
misreadings: Not a rebuke of the wronged person's feelings; it is about what anger does to judgement.
cautions: Spoken to Draupadi, whose anger was just. Do not turn it on a reader who has been wronged and is angry about it.
speaks_to: someone who regrets things said in a fight
a hot temper at work or home
not_for: a reader whose anger at real injustice is being dismissed by others

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.30.9 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXIX.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Draupadi: correct.
translation_note: Accurate; matches BORI (ātmānaṃ ca paraṃ caiva). Sanskrit typo in our text: 'दूयोरेष' should be 'द्वयोरेष' (dvayor eṣa).
context: Part of Yudhishthira's case against anger. Right after this verse he adds that a weak man who flares up against a stronger persecutor destroys himself, and that the wise man who does not let persecution rouse his anger rejoices hereafter, having passed over his persecutor with indifference.
core_teaching: Not answering anger with anger protects both people; the one who stays calm acts like a doctor to both.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one who does not react against an enraged man saves himself and others from great fear and is the physician of both; the passage then advises the weak to suppress anger toward the strong.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.9 matches (paraṃ, 'the other'). The following verses about the weak man and the persecutor are also in the critical text.

practical_reading: In a heated exchange, the person who refuses to escalate often ends the fight for both; calm can be a form of care.
misreadings: Not an instruction to stay with an abusive person and absorb their rage.
cautions: The surrounding verses tell a weak person persecuted by a stronger one to swallow their anger; this can harm a reader in an abusive or unsafe situation. Keep the misuse note.
speaks_to: arguments with a partner, parent or colleague that keep escalating
someone who wants to be the calmer person
not_for: a reader in an abusive relationship
workplace harassment

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.30.17 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXIX.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Draupadi: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Sanskrit typo: 'वस्तु' should be 'यस्तु' (yas tu). BORI reads pratibādhate and vidvāṃso (we have paribādhate, viduṣo); same meaning.
context: Draupadi has argued that a king without tejas (fiery energy) is despised. Yudhishthira redefines tejas: the wise do not count outward wrath as strength; the truly tejasvin is the one who restrains anger as it arises. He adds that the ignorant mistake anger for energy.

key_terms.sense: one with true power, fiery energy
those who see things as they are

core_teaching: Real strength is mastering anger with insight the moment it arises, not displaying it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders tejas as force of character: the learned credit it to one who suppresses risen wrath by wisdom, and he adds that the ignorant mistake anger for energy.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.17 has the same sense; the chapter is Yudhishthira's sustained answer to Draupadi's praise of tejas in 3.29.

practical_reading: The moment anger flares is the moment that tests strength; noticing it and steadying it is the strong act.
misreadings: Not a claim that feeling anger is weakness; the point is what one does with it.
cautions: One side of a debate; Draupadi and Bhima reply, and the epic does not simply endorse Yudhishthira.
speaks_to: a leader or parent who wants to model calm strength
not_for: a reader being told their justified anger is a character flaw

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.30.25 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXIX.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Draupadi: correct.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira argues that if the injured always returned injury and the punished always punished back, people would destroy one another and even birth would fail; the world continues only because some are as forgiving as the earth. He goes on to say one should forgive every injury, then quotes Kashyapa's verses on kshama.
core_teaching: Peace among people depends on some who absorb injury without retaliating; quarrels grow from anger and end through forbearance.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it within a chain: if injury were always returned, fathers, sons and spouses would slay each other and creatures could not be born; the earth-like forgiving keep life going.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.25 matches; 3.30.31 restates that creatures live because forgiving people like the earth exist.

practical_reading: Someone has to be the first to stop returning the hurt; in families and friendships that choice is often what keeps the relationship alive.
misreadings: Not a demand that one person in a relationship absorb all the harm.
cautions: The same speech says one should forgive under every injury, which Prahlada's limits in 3.28 contradict; do not present it as the epic's final word.
not_for: a reader in an abusive or exploitative relationship

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.30.37 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXIX.
attribution_note: Correct nesting: verses sung by the sage Kashyapa, quoted by Yudhishthira to Draupadi.
translation_note: Accurate. BORI reads kṣamayā coddhṛtaṃ jagat ('by forbearance the world is upheld') for our kṣamayedaṃ dhṛtaṃ jagat; same sense. 'kṣamā brahma' could also be 'forbearance is Brahman (the Veda/absolute)'.
context: Having argued that forgiveness keeps the world alive, Yudhishthira quotes Kashyapa's gatha: forgiveness is dharma, sacrifice, the Vedas, Brahman, truth, austerity, purity, and what upholds the world; the forgiving reach the highest worlds. He ends by urging Draupadi to let go of her anger, expecting Bhishma, Krishna, Vidura and others to press Dhritarashtra for peace.

key_terms.sense: the sacred, the absolute (or the Veda)

core_teaching: Praise poetry that identifies forbearance with every high value: truth, discipline, purity, the sacred itself. It is what holds the world together.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli presents it as Kashyapa's hymn: forgiveness is virtue, sacrifice, Veda, Brahma, truth, stored merit, asceticism and holiness, and the world is held together by it; the forgiving attain Brahma's world.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.36-39; c-pada reads kṣamayā coddhṛtaṃ jagat. 3.30.39 adds that kshama is the energy of the energetic.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Quotes these verses, then argues Yudhishthira's forgiveness here was partly calculation about Kaurava strength, and that Draupadi and Bhima saw it as confusion; Vyasa then sends Arjuna for weapons.

practical_reading: Forbearance is presented not as weakness but as a discipline as demanding as any austerity; choosing it can be an act of strength.
misreadings: Not an obligation to forgive someone who is still harming you.
Not the epic's conclusion: Draupadi and Bhima answer it, and Prahlada's limits stand.
cautions: High praise of forgiveness can feel like pressure to a reader who is not ready; keep the misuse note.
speaks_to: someone who has chosen to forgive and wants to understand that choice as strength
not_for: fresh betrayal or ongoing abuse
a reader being pressured by others to 'just forgive'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.32.2-3 (BORI critical edition; our Sanskrit spans two verses); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXXI.
attribution_note: Yudhishthira to Draupadi: correct. Setting is right: in the previous chapter (BORI 3.31, Ganguli XXX) Draupadi blamed the Creator for letting the good suffer.
translation_note: Accurate for 3.32.2, but the second verse (3.32.3) is only partly rendered; it adds 'whether there is a fruit or not, I do as best I can what a householder ought to do'. Sanskrit typo: 'चराम्भुत' should be 'चराम्युत' (carāmy uta). BORI reads dharmaphalānveṣī for our dharmaphalākāṅkṣī (same sense).
context: Draupadi has protested that the Ordainer treats people like puppets, rewarding the wicked and crushing the good. Yudhishthira calls her speech fine but faithless (nāstikya) and answers that he does not practise dharma for its fruit: he gives because giving is due and sacrifices because sacrifice is due. He goes on to warn against doubting dharma and insists that dharma does bear fruit, even if its workings are hidden.

key_terms.sense: one who seeks the reward of righteousness
what ought to be given / offered
what ought to be done, duty
denial or doubt of dharma's order

core_teaching: Right action is done because it is right, not as a trade for reward. Yudhishthira still holds that dharma bears fruit; it is just not his motive.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: he acts from duty, not for fruits, following scripture and the conduct of the good; whoever wants dharma's fruits is a 'trader in virtue', and he then urges Draupadi not to doubt that virtue bears fruit.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the explicit 'trader in dharma' line is only a starred insertion (*0111); the constituted text makes the same point at 3.32.5: one who tries to milk dharma does not obtain its fruit.

practical_reading: Do the decent thing because it is decent, not because it will be noticed or repaid; this guards against bitterness when good acts go unrewarded.
misreadings: Not a claim that goodness has no results; Yudhishthira says it does.
Not a dismissal of Draupadi's suffering; it answers her theology, not her pain.
cautions: Said in reply to a woman in exile protesting injustice; avoid using it to tell a suffering reader that complaining is faithless.
speaks_to: someone whose good deeds go unthanked
burnout from doing right and seeing others prosper by doing wrong
not_for: a reader angry at real injustice who needs their protest heard first

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.33.12 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXXII.
attribution_note: Draupadi to Yudhishthira: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. BORI reads upāsīno ... svapet ... ivāmbhasi for our upāsīta ... svapan ... ivodake; same image.
context: Draupadi apologises for seeming to slander dharma but presses her point: every living thing must act; only the immobile live without acting. Those who trust only fate and those who trust only chance are the worst of people; the one who believes in effort is praised. She credits this teaching to a learned Brahmin, reciting Brihaspati's doctrine, whom she heard in her father's house.
core_teaching: Waiting on fate without effort leads to ruin; human effort is required alongside whatever destiny brings.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: believers in destiny and in chance are both the worst of men; one who lies idle trusting destiny perishes like an unburnt pot in water; only those who trust in action deserve praise.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.33.12; the surrounding chapter weighs daiva (fate), haṭha (chance) and puruṣakāra (effort) and concludes one must act.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Reads Draupadi's speech as a call to act now: only the immobile can live without acting, and believers in destiny or chance are both wrong.

practical_reading: Hoping things will change is not a plan; take the next concrete step yourself.
misreadings: Not a claim that outcomes are fully in our control; the same speech says success depends on many factors.
cautions: The 'fool' language can shame a reader who is stuck because of depression or illness rather than idleness.
speaks_to: someone ready to stop waiting and start
not_for: a reader paralysed by depression or grief who needs gentleness, not a push

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.33.45-46 (BORI critical edition; two verses); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXXII.
attribution_note: Draupadi to Yudhishthira: correct.
translation_note: Accurate in sense. Our Sanskrit has 'tat kṛtaṃ saphalaṃ mayā' and 'taccedaṃ phalam'; BORI reads 'kṛtaṃ tat sakalaṃ mayā' ('I have done all of it') and 'tac ced aphalam' ('if it is fruitless'); the translation follows the critical sense.
context: Draupadi illustrates effort and what lies beyond it: the farmer breaks the soil, sows, and then waits, because rain is the cause he cannot supply (3.33.44). If rain fails, he is blameless; he tells himself he did all a person could, and the wise do not reproach themselves. She then says not to despair when effort does not succeed.
core_teaching: Do your full share of the work; when an outcome depends on forces beyond you and fails, you are not at fault and should not condemn yourself.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the tiller ploughs and sows and then sits silent, the clouds being the cause; if they fail him he is absolved, tells himself he did what others do, and does not indulge in self-reproach.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.33.44-46 has the full image (ploughing, sowing, waiting on Parjanya); the next verses list success as depending on many factors combined.

practical_reading: After giving something your honest best, separate what was yours to do from what was not; failure in the second part is not a verdict on you.
misreadings: Not an excuse for half-effort; the farmer did everything others do.
cautions: Gentle and widely usable; careful only when the 'outcome' is a death or illness, where 'not your fault' must not sound dismissive.
speaks_to: self-blame after a failed exam, interview, venture or pregnancy attempt
caregivers who did everything and still lost
not_for: a reader who has not yet tried and is looking for permission not to

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.33.47 (BORI critical edition, a three-line verse); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. XXXII.
attribution_note: Draupadi to Yudhishthira: correct.
translation_note: Acceptable. BORI's third line (47e) says the result is either success or non-success, while non-action is otherwise, which supports our 'only by not acting is the outcome certain'. Our Sanskrit (dvāv antau yasya) omits that line. Ganguli reads 'dvau' differently: there are two other causes of success besides effort.
context: Right after the farmer image, Draupadi says no one should fall into despair saying 'I work and do not succeed'. Success comes from many factors together; if one is missing the result is reduced or absent, but without beginning there is no fruit at all. The wise bring together place, time, means and auspicious circumstance as best they can.

key_terms.sense: two outcomes (success or failure) / two factors

core_teaching: Lack of success so far is no reason to despair; action can go either way, but not acting guarantees no result.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should not despair at acting without success, because there are two other causes besides exertion; success depends on a union of circumstances, but without exertion there can be none.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.33.47-48: effort ends in success or non-success, non-action in neither; results come from many factors combined, and with no undertaking there is no fruit.

practical_reading: Keep going after setbacks: each try carries a real chance, while giving up removes it.
misreadings: Not a promise that persistence always pays off.
cautions: For someone exhausted by repeated failure (e.g. long job search, infertility), pair with rest and with 3.32.48's 'do not blame yourself'.
not_for: situations where stopping is the wise and healthy choice

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.57.13 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. LX (our verified_with says LIX; the dice game begins in LIX, this line is in LX).
attribution_note: Wrong speaker. This is Damayanti speaking to Nala's charioteer Varshneya (BORI 3.57.11-13; Ganguli LX), inside the sage Brihadashva's narration to Yudhishthira. Fix: speaker 'Damayanti', listener 'Varshneya, Nala's charioteer'; nested in Brihadashva's tale to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate (BORI: puṣkareṇeha; dyūte vai). Ganguli renders rāga as 'ardour for the play'.
context: Kali has entered Nala and Pushkara keeps winning with Kali's help; for months Nala gambles away gold, chariots and robes and will not see his ministers or citizens. Damayanti summons the charioteer Varshneya and tells him the more Nala loses, the stronger his passion for the dice, that he no longer heeds friends or even her. She asks Varshneya to take their two children to her father in Vidarbha.
core_teaching: Losses can feed a compulsion rather than stop it; Damayanti sees the pattern clearly and acts to protect her children.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. LX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the line to Damayanti, speaking to Varshneya: the more the king loses to Pushkara, the greater his ardour for play, and he heeds neither friends nor her; she sends the children to safety.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.57.11-16 frames it as bhaimī uvāca to Vārṣṇeya; the verse continues that the dice obey Pushkara and turn against Nala, and that he no longer listens to friends.

practical_reading: Chasing losses is a known trap: the more one loses, the harder stopping feels. Damayanti's response models seeing it clearly and protecting those who depend on you.
misreadings: Not a moral verdict on Nala's character; the text attributes the compulsion to Kali's possession, and he later recovers.
cautions: Gambling and addiction; avoid shaming language toward someone with a compulsion.
The story continues with Nala abandoning Damayanti in the forest.
speaks_to: someone watching a loved one spiral into gambling or another compulsion
someone noticing their own 'chasing losses' pattern
not_for: using it to label a person with addiction as weak or bad

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.58.27-28 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. LXI. Our Sanskrit blends Damayanti's line (BORI 3.58.27) with Nala's reply (3.58.28c).
attribution_note: Mostly correct: Damayanti speaks to Nala. But in BORI and Ganguli the phrase 'for a man in distress' (narasyārtasya bheṣajam) is in Nala's agreeing reply; Damayanti's own line says physicians hold there is no medicine like a wife in every sorrow.
translation_note: Accurate to our (vulgate) text. Sanskrit typo: 'सत्यमेतद्व्रवीमि' should be 'सत्यमेतद्ब्रवीमि'. Damayanti appeals to 'the physicians' opinion' (bhiṣajāṃ matam) in BORI.
context: Having lost his kingdom, Nala wanders the forest with Damayanti, half-starved, and keeps pointing out the road to Vidarbha. She fears he means to send her away and says she will soothe his weariness, since nothing heals sorrow like a wife. Nala agrees and swears he would sooner give up himself than her, yet that same night, still under Kali's influence, he cuts her half-garment and abandons her as she sleeps.
core_teaching: In hardship, a loving companion is the best medicine. Damayanti offers herself as that companion when Nala has lost everything.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. LXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Damayanti says physicians hold that in every sorrow nothing equals a wife; Nala agrees there is no friend or medicine like a wife for a man in distress, and swears not to forsake her.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text: Damayanti 3.58.27 (no remedy like a wife, physicians say); Nala 3.58.28 (no friend or medicine like a wife for the distressed). Our verse merges the two.

practical_reading: When someone you love has lost everything, staying close can matter more than advice; a steady companion is itself a kind of medicine.
misreadings: Not a claim that a wife exists to heal her husband; our line rightly widens it to any partner.
cautions: Right after this, Nala abandons her; a reader who was left by a partner may find it painful.
Gendered frame (wife as medicine for a man); keep our gender-neutral line.
speaks_to: standing by a partner through job loss, debt or illness
feeling grateful for a partner who stayed
not_for: someone recently abandoned or widowed
someone pressured to stay with a partner who harms them

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.131.12 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CXXXI.
attribution_note: Speaker correct (the hawk, Indra in disguise), but the listener in this passage is King Ushinara, not Shibi (BORI 3.130.17-19, 3.131.22, 26; Ganguli CXXX-CXXXI). The tale is told by the sage Lomasha to Yudhishthira at the Jala and Upajala rivers. The version with Shibi Aushinara (Ushinara's son) is a separate telling at BORI 3.197, narrated by Markandeya. Fix the listener and the prasang title, or move the verse to the Shibi telling.
translation_note: Accurate. The hawk's argument just before (3.131.10-11) is essential: a dharma that obstructs another dharma is no dharma; weigh the conflicting duties and follow the one that harms none.
context: Indra as a hawk and Agni as a dove test King Ushinara at his sacrifice. The dove takes refuge on the king's thigh; the hawk claims it as his ordained food and argues that saving one bird will starve him and his family, so the king must weigh the duties and choose the weightier. The king replies that abandoning a refugee is the gravest wrong, offers anything else, and finally puts his own flesh on the scale until he climbs on himself; the gods reveal themselves and bless him.

key_terms.sense: deciding what is right and wrong

core_teaching: When duties conflict, weigh them and follow the one that carries more weight. The story shows the principle is sound but can be used to tempt; the king honours it by paying the cost himself rather than giving up the one who trusted him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXXXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the hawk's case: a virtue that blocks another virtue is not virtue; compare opposing duties and adopt the preponderant. The king suspects the hawk is Garuda and still refuses to abandon a refugee.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.131.10-12 (hawk) and 3.130.17-19 name the king Ushinara; Shibi's own telling is at 3.197.

commentaries.who: Adam Bowles, 'The failure of dharma', Seminar 608 (2010)
commentaries.gist: Argues the epic's leitmotif is the subtlety of dharma, shown through dilemmas in which each option conforms to some dharmic norm; this hawk-and-dove dilemma fits that pattern.

practical_reading: Faced with two real obligations, slow down and weigh them honestly rather than grabbing the convenient one; be wary when the 'greater good' happens to cost someone else everything.
misreadings: Not a license to sacrifice a vulnerable person for the many; the king refuses exactly that.
The speaker uses the principle to tempt; do not present it as the story's moral without the king's answer.
cautions: The story ends with the king cutting his own flesh; avoid literal self-sacrifice imagery for a reader at risk of self-harm.
speaks_to: a hard choice between two obligations (family vs work, two people who need you)
a promise to someone who trusted you
not_for: someone being pressured to give up a dependent or a promise 'for the greater good'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.133.9 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CXXXIII.
attribution_note: Ashtavakra to the gatekeeper at Janaka's sacrifice: correct. Nested: Lomasha tells the story to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate in sense. The image is of the silk-cotton (śālmali) tree, whose swollen knots do not show its age; the fruit-bearing tree, however small, counts as grown.
context: Ashtavakra, born bent in eight places by his father Kahoda's curse, learns in his twelfth year that Kahoda was defeated in debate by Bandin at King Janaka's court and made to enter the water. With his uncle Shvetaketu he goes to Janaka's sacrifice; the gatekeeper bars boys and asks him to recite a hard verse. Ashtavakra answers that growth is not measured by bodily size, then that grey hair does not make an elder, and is admitted.
core_teaching: Maturity is shown by what a person produces in wisdom and conduct, not by age or size.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it: true growth cannot be inferred from bodily development, as knots on the Salmali do not show its age; a slender, short tree bearing fruit is full-grown, a fruitless one is not.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.133.9, a trishtubh verse in the same wording; the gatekeeper's challenge and Ashtavakra's replies run through 3.133.

practical_reading: Judge people, including yourself, by the fruit of their lives rather than by age, size or title.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of elders; Ashtavakra himself honours learning.
cautions: Mild. The frame story involves a father's curse and apparent drowning.
speaks_to: someone who feels small next to bigger peers
not_for: a reader using it to wave away experienced advice

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.133.11 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CXXXIII. Parallel: Manusmriti 2.156.
attribution_note: Ashtavakra to the gatekeeper: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our note's Manu 2.156 parallel is confirmed (Manu reads 'na tena vṛddho bhavati' and 'yo vai yuvāpy adhīyānaḥ').
context: The gatekeeper has said boys learn from the old and only grow wise with time. Ashtavakra replies that grey hair does not make an elder; the gods count the young who understand as elders; sages measure greatness by learning, not years, wealth or kin. He then asks to be announced to Janaka and goes on to defeat Bandin, which frees his father.
core_teaching: Seniority belongs to understanding, not to age; a young person who knows is an elder in the eyes of the gods.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one is not old because his head is grey; the gods count as old the child who has knowledge; sages do not measure merit by years, grey hair, wealth or friends.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on the parallel Manusmriti 2.156 (tr. Ganganath Jha)
commentaries.gist: Explains that grey hair alone does not make one venerable; the young person who keeps studying is called an elder by the gods, and since the gods know all, the verse is praise of the learner.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.133.11 matches our Sanskrit.

practical_reading: Listen to wisdom wherever it comes from, including from people much younger than you; age earns respect, but understanding earns authority.
misreadings: Not contempt for the old; it denies that age alone confers wisdom.
cautions: None significant.
speaks_to: a young person whose ideas are dismissed
an older person learning from the young
not_for: a reader using it to justify disrespect toward elders

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.149.26 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CXLIX (our verified_with says CL).
attribution_note: Hanuman to Bhima: correct. Setting is roughly right: it comes as Hanuman sends Bhima on to the Saugandhika grove, after his long teaching on the ages and the orders.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Searching for the Saugandhika flower for Draupadi, Bhima finds an old monkey blocking his path and cannot lift its tail; it is his brother Hanuman, who shows his giant form and teaches about the yugas and the duties of the orders. Sending him on, Hanuman warns him not to take the flowers by force from Kubera's garden, to keep to his own dharma, and adds this verse; next he says that wrong sometimes passes under the name of right and right under the name of wrong.

key_terms.sense: equal to Brihaspati, guru of the gods

core_teaching: Knowing what is right needs study and the company of experienced elders; brilliance alone is not enough.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXLIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: without knowing duties and serving the old, even someone like Brihaspati cannot understand profit and religion; one must discriminate cases where vice passes as virtue and virtue as vice.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.149.26. The apparatus shows a near-identical line in a Southern insertion in Vidura's counsel (Udyoga 5.39), about learning that is not understood without serving elders.

practical_reading: Before acting on a strong conviction, test it with people who have lived through similar choices.
misreadings: Not blind deference to anyone older.
cautions: None significant; context is a gentle teaching after humbling Bhima's pride.
speaks_to: a capable person tempted to go it alone
after being humbled by a mistake
not_for: situations where 'elders' are the source of harm

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.178.5 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CLXXX.
attribution_note: Wrong speaker. Yudhishthira asks the question (3.178.3: which is weightier, giving or truth, harmlessness or kind speech?) and the serpent Nahusha answers with this verse. Fix: speaker 'Nahusha (as the serpent)', listener 'Yudhishthira'. Our_note ('Yudhishthira on the relative weight of virtues') should also be corrected.
translation_note: Accurate for the verse, but the second sentence of our translation ('harmlessness can matter more than pleasant speech... depends on what the situation requires') renders the next verses (3.178.6-7), not this Sanskrit.
context: The python holding Bhima is King Nahusha, cursed by Agastya. He agrees to free Bhima if Yudhishthira answers his questions; after an exchange on who is a Brahmin, Yudhishthira in turn asks him what leads to the highest state. Nahusha names giving to the worthy, kind speech, truth and harmlessness; asked which weighs more, he answers that it depends on the weight of the task at hand.

key_terms.sense: the greater weight of what the situation requires

core_teaching: No single virtue always outranks another; their relative weight depends on what the situation demands.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the answer to the snake: the relative merit of truth, charity, kind speech and harmlessness is measured by their gravity in effect; sometimes truth, sometimes giving, is the more praiseworthy.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.3-7: Yudhishthira asks, the serpent (sarpa uvāca) answers that weight depends on the task (kāryagarīyastva, kāryāpekṣam).

practical_reading: When two good values pull apart, such as honesty and kindness, ask which one the situation actually needs most rather than applying a fixed rule.
misreadings: Not moral relativism; all four virtues remain binding, only their ranking shifts.
cautions: None significant.
speaks_to: ethical dilemmas at work or home
choosing between telling a hard truth and being generous
not_for: someone looking for permission to lie

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.178.30 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CLXXX.
attribution_note: Nahusha (as the serpent) to Yudhishthira: correct.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Yudhishthira, impressed by the serpent's learning, asks how delusion could overtake one so wise who once lived in heaven. Nahusha answers with this verse and confesses that the intoxication of power made him fall; now awakened, he is teaching Yudhishthira. He then tells how he made sages carry his palanquin and touched Agastya with his foot.
core_teaching: Success can cloud the judgement even of the wise and brave, and the one living in comfort does not notice it happening.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: prosperity intoxicates even the wise and valiant, and those in luxury lose their reason; Nahusha says he too fell this way and, restored to awareness, now instructs Yudhishthira.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.30. A Southern insertion (BORI Appendix I.20) expands it: pride sits in power as surely as heat in fire, and an eye darkened by power regains clarity only after the salve of a fall.

practical_reading: Good times are exactly when to check yourself: ask trusted people whether success has changed how you treat others.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of success itself.
cautions: None significant.
speaks_to: after a fall from a high position
not_for: someone in poverty or failure, for whom it may sound like 'better that you didn't succeed'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.178.33 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CLXXX.
attribution_note: Nahusha to Yudhishthira: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Sanskrit typo: 'विमानन' should be 'विमानेन' (vimānena).
context: Nahusha's confession: ruling heaven in Indra's place, he travelled in a celestial car, took tribute from sages, gods and every being, and drained the power of anyone he looked at. A thousand brahmarshis carried his palanquin; he touched Agastya with his foot and was cursed to fall as a serpent. Agastya told him Yudhishthira would release him.

key_terms.sense: I gave no thought to anyone else

core_teaching: Pride at the height of power made Nahusha blind to others, and that blindness caused his fall.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: revelling in pride in his celestial car he thought of nothing else, exacted tribute from all three worlds, had Brahmarshis draw his car, and was cursed when his foot touched Agastya.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.33-38 gives the confession in the same order; Udyoga 5.11-17 tells the fuller story of Nahusha's rise and fall.

practical_reading: Notice when you stop thinking about the people who carry you; that loss of attention is an early sign of pride.
misreadings: Not a story about divine punishment for success; the fault is contempt for others.
cautions: None significant.
speaks_to: someone reflecting honestly on past arrogance
not_for: a reader already crushed by shame who needs mercy more than a mirror

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.178.43 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CLXXX.
attribution_note: Nahusha to Yudhishthira: correct.
translation_note: Two textual points. BORI reads dānanityatā ('constancy in giving') where our Sanskrit has jñānanityatā ('constancy in knowledge'), and sadā puṃsām ('always, for people') for our satāṃ puṃsām. Sādhakāni means 'what brings people to their goal' (Ganguli: the means of securing salvation), so 'what make a person good' slightly shifts the sense.
context: Nahusha has just described how Agastya's curse and his promise of release showed him the power of tapas and of true brahmanhood. He concludes that truth, self-control, austerity, yoga, harmlessness and constant giving (or knowledge) are what bring people to their goal, not birth or family. He then releases Bhima and rises to heaven.

key_terms.sense: means of accomplishment, what brings one to the goal

core_teaching: What brings a person to the highest good is cultivated character and practice, not birth or family.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: truth, charity, self-restraint, penance, harmlessness and constancy in virtue, not race or family connections, are the means by which a man must always secure salvation.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.43 reads dānanityatā and sadā puṃsām. Earlier in the same dialogue (3.177) Yudhishthira argues a Brahmin is known by conduct, not birth.

practical_reading: What you practise every day, honesty, restraint, kindness, generosity, shapes you more than where you come from.
misreadings: Do not present the epic as uniformly anti-caste; the same dialogue also says mixing has made birth hard to determine.
cautions: Caste is a sensitive topic; keep the focus on conduct over birth without making broad historical claims.
speaks_to: someone judged by background or family
not_for: none in particular

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.187.42 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CLXXXVIII (our verified_with says CLXXXIX).
attribution_note: Correct, but nested: the child (Narayana) speaks to Markandeya inside Markandeya's own account to the Pandavas. Speaker/listener fields are fine; add the nesting.
translation_note: Accurate. Viklava = agitated, distressed, unnerved. Sanskrit spelling: 'विक्लबोसि' is normally 'विक्लवोऽसि'.
context: Markandeya tells the Pandavas of the end of an age: the world became one ocean and he wandered alone, exhausted, finding no rest, until he saw a radiant child on a banyan bough. The child drew him in through his mouth, and inside he saw all the worlds intact; then he was released. The child, revealing himself as Narayana, explains that he showed the universe because he knew Markandeya's distress at seeing everything destroyed.

key_terms.sense: all moving and unmoving beings destroyed

core_teaching: God notices the distress of the one who feels alone in a destroyed world and answers it by showing that nothing is truly lost; all is held within him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: seeing one expanse of water and all creatures destroyed, Markandeya was afflicted with melancholy; knowing this, the Lord showed him the universe within his body, then brought him out.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 12.9 (Bhaktivedanta VedaBase), parallel telling
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata version has Markandeya ask to see the Lord's illusory power; he is drawn in by the infant's breath, sees the universe intact, and feels lamentation and bewilderment before the vision ends.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.187.42; Markandeya's vision runs through 3.186-187.

practical_reading: When everything familiar seems swept away, the story offers the image of being seen in one's fear and shown that what matters is still held somewhere.
misreadings: Not a promise that what was lost will be restored in the same form.
cautions: Imagery of total destruction; can resonate with catastrophic loss (disaster, death of many). Keep the comfort in 'you were seen', not in 'it will all come back'.
speaks_to: feeling utterly alone in a crisis
not_for: fresh bereavement where 'all is preserved' may sound dismissive

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.187.55 (BORI critical edition); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CLXXXVIII.

key_terms.sense: the one fit to give refuge

core_teaching: Krishna is parent to every being and the proper refuge; the sage invites the Pandavas to take shelter in him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Markandeya says this Madhava is father and mother of all creatures and bids the Kuru bulls seek his refuge; they and Draupadi bow down and Krishna consoles them.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)

practical_reading: For a devotional reader, it invites trust: the divine is as near and caring as a parent.
misreadings: Not a substitute for practical help or care.
cautions: Parent imagery can be painful for a reader with an absent or harmful parent; offer it as what a parent should be.
not_for: a non-devotional reader who wants practical guidance

verified_ref: Mahabharata 3.198.40c-41a (BORI critical edition; our Sanskrit spans two half-verses); Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CCVI.
attribution_note: Correct, but nested three deep: Vaishampayana narrates to Janamejaya; Markandeya tells the story to Yudhishthira; within it the Dharmavyadha teaches the Brahmin Kaushika.

context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should never cast off virtue from lust, wrath or malice, never joy immoderately at good fortune or grieve immoderately at bad, and never leave virtue when poverty comes.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga, 'What is Duty?' (Complete Works vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Retells the Vyadha story to argue that doing the duty of one's station wholeheartedly and without attachment to results leads to the highest realisation; no duty is impure.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.40-41; the whole chapter is the Vyadha's account of śiṣṭācāra.

practical_reading: Name the feeling that is pushing you to cut a corner (wanting, anger, resentment) and decide not to let it make the choice; likewise, ride highs and lows without being carried off.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all emotion; it warns against over-reacting and against letting feelings override principle.
cautions: For someone in fresh grief, 'do not burn with distress' can sound like 'do not grieve'; avoid that framing.
speaks_to: holding steady through good and bad news
not_for: fresh bereavement

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.42-43, same wording.

those who see the real meaning of things
putting that friendship forward, on the strength of it

core_teaching: A short shared walk already creates a bond; on that basis Savitri earns the right to be heard even by Death.

the timeless way of the good

context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Satisfied, the Yaksha lets him choose one brother to revive. He chooses Nakula. context: Thirteen years after the dice game, the Pandavas ask for their kingdom back. Yudhishthira replies (sec. XXVIII) that dharma must be discerned, not assumed, and defers to Krishna, who (sec. XXIX) defends the Pandavas' claim and blames the Kauravas' greed.
